meta_desc: NCERT Exemplar Class 12 Q2 solved: prove ∫(2x+3)/(x²+3x) dx = log|x²+3x| + C via the f'(x)/f(x) log rule. Free 8-question quiz to practise.

quiz.title: f'(x)/f(x) Integration Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on spotting when the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so the integral becomes a natural log. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Integrals of the form ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = log|f(x)| + C

questions.q: Which standard result lets you solve ∫(2x+3)/(x²+3x) dx directly?
questions.explanation: The numerator 2x+3 is exactly the derivative of the denominator x²+3x, so the integral fits ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = log|f(x)| + C.

questions.q: For f(x) = x² + 3x, what is f'(x)?
questions.explanation: Differentiate term by term: d/dx(x²) = 2x and d/dx(3x) = 3, giving f'(x) = 2x + 3, which matches the numerator.
With numerator = derivative of denominator, the integral is log of the absolute value of the denominator: log|x²+3x| + C.

questions.q: Which substitution turns ∫(2x+3)/(x²+3x) dx into ∫(1/t) dt?
questions.explanation: Let t = x²+3x, then dt = (2x+3) dx. The integral becomes ∫(1/t) dt = log|t| + C = log|x²+3x| + C.
The numerator 2x is the derivative of x²+1, so ∫(2x)/(x²+1) dx = log|x²+1| + C.

questions.q: ∫ tan x dx = ∫(sin x)/(cos x) dx. What is the result?
questions.explanation: Here f(x) = cos x and f'(x) = −sin x, so ∫(sin x)/(cos x) dx = −log|cos x| + C = log|sec x| + C.

questions.q: Why does the answer carry an absolute value, log|x²+3x| rather than log(x²+3x)?
options: To make the answer look longer
Because the constant C requires it
Because x²+3x can be negative, and log is defined only for positive arguments
It is optional and can be dropped
questions.explanation: The expression x²+3x is negative for −3 < x < 0, so the modulus keeps the logarithm's argument positive and the result valid on every interval.
d/dx(x³+2x) = 3x²+2, which is the numerator, so the integral is log|x³+2x| + C.

faq.q: How do you know to use the log rule for ∫(2x+3)/(x²+3x) dx?
faq.a: Differentiate the denominator: d/dx(x²+3x) = 2x+3, which is exactly the numerator. Whenever the top is the derivative of the bottom, the integral is log of the bottom.

faq.q: What is the general rule being applied here?
faq.a: ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = log|f(x)| + C. Set t = f(x) so dt = f'(x) dx, and the integral collapses to ∫(1/t) dt = log|t| + C.

faq.q: Why does the answer use log|x²+3x| with a modulus?
faq.a: Because x²+3x is negative for −3 < x < 0, and the logarithm needs a positive argument. The absolute value keeps the result valid across all intervals of x.

faq.q: Do I need partial fractions for this integral?
faq.a: No. Partial fractions would work but are unnecessary once you spot that the numerator is the derivative of the denominator — the log rule gives the answer in one step.
